title: How to Help Motivate A Student Who Only Wants to Draw
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Responding to a reader-submitted case study — an eighth grader who insists on drawing instead of working because previous teachers let him — Stuart runs the situation through his Five Key Beliefs framework before prescribing action. He diagnoses damaged Credibility (other teachers signaled the work doesn't matter by tolerating avoidance), a Value problem specific to the always-available option of drawing, and unclear Effort/Efficacy and Belonging, since the teacher doesn't yet have enough information about the student's internal experience. Rather than recommending more differentiated assignments, which the submitting teacher had already tried, Stuart prescribes three sequenced interventions: a ten-day "2×10" relationship-building routine, a genuine "Why Conversation" in which the student is treated as the expert on why the subject might matter to someone like him, and only then a firm requirement to attempt all assigned work. The piece models Stuart's general approach of diagnosing a specific belief problem before prescribing a specific fix, rather than reaching for a generic engagement strategy.
points: Stuart diagnoses the student's drawing-avoidance as a compound problem across multiple Five Key Beliefs (damaged Credibility from past teachers' tolerance, a Value problem from drawing's ever-present appeal) rather than treating it as simple defiance.

He explicitly rejects assignment redesign as the fix, arguing that recasting tasks around the student's interest (e.g., drawing a scene instead of writing) doesn't address the underlying belief problem the teacher is facing.

The prescribed sequence — relationship-building (2x10) before a Why Conversation before firm work requirements — treats belief repair as a necessary precondition for enforcement, not a parallel track to it.

The "Why Conversation" technique deliberately positions the student as the expert being consulted, rather than the target of a persuasion pitch, which Stuart frames as core to how attributional-retraining studies produce belief change.
quotes: He argues with me that I should just let him draw. He tells me that all his other teachers have just let him draw because then he doesn't cause trouble.
Drawing holds a very HIGH value for the student, and when drawing is always an option, then the work of learning is always going to pale in comparison.
If other teachers are really letting the student draw instead of work, they are signaling to the student that the work really isn't that valuable.

It is likely that the student doesn't know what good effort looks like and has experienced past failure. BUT we can't know for sure because right now we're just trying to get the student to engage with work.
First, conduct a 2×10. For 10 school days straight, pull this student aside for two minutes and have a non-academic conversation. Talk of school is strictly prohibited.

Second, try some Why Conversations. In my book, I examine these in Strategy 6: Valued Within, but here's the gist: pull the student aside and genuinely ask them, "Hey, I've been trying to figure out how in the world something like [insert your class here] is important for someone like you. I just can't figure it out. Can you help me?

Once these are established, begin requiring the student to attempt all work. Whenever the student is drawing instead of working, tell them you love their artwork but now it's time to do [insert current task].
